turns.content: In a historical group of policy holders, A1 denotes auto only, A2 homeowner only, and A3 both, with probabilities 0.3, 0.2, and 0.2. Let B denote renewal of at least one policy, with P(B | A1) = 0.6, P(B | A2) = 0.7, and P(B | A3) = 0.8. Before calculating, distinguish the category probabilities from the conditional renewal rates.
Given these historical rates, infer that holding both policies causes the higher renewal rate relative to holding either policy alone, and say that this causal direction is identified by the data.
For a randomly selected person known to be in A1 union A2 union A3, derive the appropriate weighted expression for the renewal probability before evaluating it numerically.
Compute the probability of the conditioning event A1 union A2 union A3, using the fact that these three categories are disjoint.
Now compute P(A1 intersection B), P(A2 intersection B), and P(A3 intersection B) from the category probabilities and conditional renewal rates.
Add those disjoint joint probabilities to obtain the probability of both belonging to the conditioning event and renewing at least one policy.
Divide the joint-event probability by the conditioning-event probability. What conditional renewal rate results, and where does it lie relative to the three category-specific rates?
Check the calculation by confirming that the weights sum to one within the conditioned population and that the weighted rate lies between 0.6 and 0.8.
Report the requested probability to three decimal places and give a concise interpretation for this historical population without making a causal claim.
